strengths: meiwaku is explained as practical trouble (sleeves, sudden stops, leftover wrappers), not as a mystical national virtue.
Stall-edge eating as part of the purchase versus a bento in a station wicket is a local distinction visitors miss.
tachi-gui versus tabearuki is correctly treated as a difference locals care about.
Spatial, not verbal, feedback on packed trains matches everyday Japanese public-space habit.

issues.location: ## How Japanese People Learn the Pause — “Outdoor eating is already a special case.”
issues.problem: Japanese readers will not recognize outdoor eating itself as rare or special: parks, riverbanks, hanami, stall edges, and konbini counters are ordinary. The article’s own FAQ later says this. Framing outdoor eating as special makes the local lens sound tourist-theoretical.
issues.suggestion: Keep seated home meals as the default indoor pattern, but say outdoor eating is common; the extra layer is eating while moving through a busy sidewalk.

issues.problem: “They usually look slightly annoyed at themselves” invents a typical facial script for locals.
issues.suggestion: Describe the situation (late, juggling rice and a wicket) without a claimed inner mood.

issues.problem: The default street is dense downtown (Harajuku, station wickets, office 8 a.m.). Smaller towns and school-route ice cream are only lightly implied.
issues.suggestion: One hedge that quieter residential streets show more casual walking snacks, especially among kids, would match local variation without a new anecdote.
